status: planning arithmetic and estimates; nothing here is simulated anew, built or measured

kinds.a: a prescribed-walk or static model result of this study
kinds.b: a closed-loop simulation result of this study
kinds.c: a sourced fact (a catalog id, a document or record of this study, or a web page)
kinds.d: an estimate or assumption (whose, and how derived, is in its basis)

web_read: read on 14 Nov 2026 through the web-search tool's extract of the page; the page itself could not be opened from the session, whose network allows the search tool only, so confirm it on the page before relying on it

feetech_sts3215_c018.interface: TTL half-duplex serial bus, 38.4 kbps-1 Mbps, IDs 0-253; 12-bit magnetic encoder

myactuator_rmd_x4_p36_36_e_l.interface: CAN bus + EtherCAT (ECAT IN/OUT); dual encoder 17-bit/18-bit

model_sensor_age_ms.note: sensors describe the last step's start

model_delay_steps_max.note: latency_steps (0, 10) in the environment and LATENCY_MAX_STEPS = 10 in the ledger: 0-20 ms

judged_delay_ms.note: P29: the bar is judged at 10 ms

frames_per_drive_per_cycle.note: a command (0x140 + ID) and its reply (0x240 + ID)

can_frame_bits_plain.note: 8 n + 47 for n = 8 data bytes, with the 3-bit intermission

can_frame_bits_stuffed.note: plus floor((34 + 8 n - 1) / 4) = 24 stuff bits at worst

leg_drive_can_fd.basis: the author's reading: the vendor's protocol extracts list classic CAN only (standard frames, DLC 8, 1 Mbit/s) and no CAN FD mode was found; the absence is an inference, to confirm with the vendor

can_fd_data_bit_rate_bps.basis: the author's choice for a hypothetical CAN FD drive: the data rate NVIDIA's guide says every transceiver reaches (jetson_can)

utilisation_ceiling.basis: the author's rule: the cycle fits if the worst-case frame time is at most the cycle; a polled bus has one master and no other traffic, but 100 % leaves no room for a resend or a status read

pcan_usb_fd_channels.note: catalog id pcan_usb_fd, a one-channel adapter

one_bus_rate_hz.basis: the author's choice: the fastest whole multiple of the model's 2 ms step that one bus carries with 12 drives at the worst stuffing (4 ms cycle)

drive_reply_turnaround_ms.basis: not found by the author in the vendor's protocol extracts: the time a drive takes to start its reply after a command. The exchange times assume it is shorter than the command burst; the bench stopwatch measures it

drive_max_command_rate_hz.basis: not found by the author in the vendor's documents: the highest rate at which a drive accepts a command and answers each one. 500 Hz is assumed to be within it; the bench soak shows whether it is

ethercat_offered.note: both leg-drive models are -E variants: CAN bus + EtherCAT

ethercat_bit_rate_bps.basis: EtherCAT's usual 100 Mbit/s Ethernet, from the author's general knowledge; not re-read

ethercat_process_bytes_per_drive.basis: the author's assumption of a cyclic synchronous mapping: control word 2, target position 4, velocity offset 4 and torque offset 2 out; status word 2, position 4, velocity 4 and torque 2 in; the vendor's mapping was not read

ethercat_overhead_bytes.basis: the Ethernet and EtherCAT frame layout from the author's general knowledge: preamble 8, Ethernet header 14, EtherCAT header 2, datagram header 10, working counter 2, checksum 4, inter-frame gap 12

ethercat_forward_us_per_drive.basis: the author's allowance for each drive's forwarding delay; not sourced

xm540_baud_default_bps.note: Baud Rate (address 8) initial value 1; 1 Mbit/s is value 3

teensy_pin_max_v.note: no pin takes more, except VIN and VUSB

sts3215_return_delay_us.basis: two third-party write-ups disagree on the factory default (0 or 500 µs; sts3215_registers); read it from the servo

aux_baud_bps.basis: the author's choice inside both servos' catalog ranges (XM540 9.6 kbps-4.5 Mbps, STS3215 38.4 kbps-1 Mbps)

aux_bits_per_byte.basis: 8 data bits with a start and a stop bit, the usual serial framing of both protocols; from the author's general knowledge

aux_rate_hz.basis: the author's plan: the neck and tail are not in the balance loop, so their targets go out every fifth leg cycle; the model updates all 14 targets at 500 Hz

u2d2_latency_timer_ms.note: set to 1 ms; 16 ms by default

tof_rate_hz.note: the most the sensor is rated for

rt_latency_reported_ms.note: worst-case wake-up latency reported on Orin modules with the real-time kernel; 0.4 ms in one report before tuning

sts3215_vendor_rated_nm.note: the spec sheet's rated torque, 10 kg cm at 12 V and 0.9 A, with no thermal definition (the catalog's vendor_rated_definition)

sts3215_stall_nm.note: 30 kg cm at 12 V, 2.7 A (catalog notes)

box_servo_sustained_of_stall.basis: PR #662's planning rule for box servos, which the study's catalog follows (designlab/data/build_catalog.py); not the author's and not a vendor figure

video_frame_ms.basis: the author's arithmetic: one frame of a phone's slow motion at 240 and at 120 frames a second

motion_mode_kp_max.basis: the author's reading of the KP range in a sibling model's manual (myactuator_sibling_manual); its units, and whether the 75 cm build's V4 and V4.1 drives share the frame, were not confirmed

motion_mode_kd_max.basis: the author's reading of the KD range in the same sibling manual (myactuator_sibling_manual); units and applicability not confirmed

compute_mcu.basis: the author's estimate for one 500 Hz step of the tracker on a 600 MHz microcontroller: the reference look-up, the targets, the ankle cap and a share of the 100 Hz feedback. No firmware exists (COMPUTE.md). The study's Python tracker takes about 0.5 ms per physics step, physics included, on the cloud machine (LESSONS_LEARNED.md 3.12)

compute_jetson.basis: the author's estimate for the same step in compiled code on one isolated Jetson core; not measured

jitter_mcu.basis: the author's estimate for a timer-interrupt loop on a microcontroller with serial and USB interrupts beside it; not measured

jitter_jetson_rt.basis: low end: third-party tests of a PREEMPT_RT kernel on Orin modules report about 0.01-0.2 ms at worst (rt_jetson). High end: the author's allowance for the Orin Nano with the GPU loaded; no published figure for this board with the GPU loaded was found

path_mcu_can.basis: the author's estimate: the microcontroller's own CAN controller, a transmit mailbox away from the bus

path_usb_can.basis: the author's estimate for one USB hop: a High-speed USB 2.0 transfer waits for a 0.125 ms microframe, then the adapter's firmware and the Linux USB stack; no measured latency of this adapter was found

path_native_can.basis: the author's estimate for a socket write through the Linux CAN driver to the Orin's own controller

path_ethercat.basis: the author's estimate for a raw Ethernet send from a real-time thread; published jitter of EtherCAT masters on other boards is 0.004-0.022 ms (ethercat_rt)

drive_can.basis: the author's estimate from a frame's end to the torque change: up to one period of the drive's outer loop, taken as 1 ms, plus the current's rise (winding L / R: 0.18 mH / 0.4 ohm = 0.45 ms on the X4-36-L and 0.51 mH / 0.41 ohm = 1.24 ms on the X6-60, catalog notes; a closed current loop is faster). The vendor's driver manuals give a position loop of 1 kHz (V3.0) or 500 Hz (V2.1) for the MC-X drivers of the earlier RMD-X generation, with 5 kHz speed and 15 kHz current loops (myactuator_mc_driver); which loop closes the motion-mode gains on the V4 and V4.1 drives is not known. With a 500 Hz loop the high end would be 2.50 ms

drive_ethercat.basis: the author's estimate: a cyclic synchronous drive takes its setpoint at its next sync event, up to one 2 ms cycle, then the torque rises as over CAN; the vendor's cycle times were not found

classic_can.arithmetic: 8 x 8 + 47 = 111 bits; + floor((34 + 8 x 8 - 1) / 4) = 24 stuff bits = 135 bits; at 1 Mbit/s one bit is 1 µs

can_fd_hypothetical.arithmetic: 30 bits at 1 Mbit/s + 96 bits at 5 Mbit/s; at worst + 4 and + 17 stuff bits

ethercat.arithmetic: 52 + 12 x 24 = 340 bytes x 8 / 100 Mbit/s + 12 x 1 µs

bus_load.bus: CAN FD, 1 and 5 Mbit/s (hypothetical: not offered by the leg drives as far as found)

A.name: Raspberry Pi 5 + Teensy 4.1, two CAN buses (COMPUTE.md's design, the baseline)
A.rate_note: Two of the Teensy's three CAN ports, one leg (6 drives) on each.

rate_held.basis: bus-time arithmetic on sourced frame lengths; it takes the drives' reply turnaround as shorter than the command burst and assumes the drives accept a command each at this rate, neither of which was found (d)

compute.basis: the author's estimate for one 500 Hz step of the tracker on a 600 MHz microcontroller: the reference look-up, the targets, the ankle cap and a share of the 100 Hz feedback. No firmware exists (COMPUTE.md). The study's Python tracker takes about 0.5 ms per physics step, physics included, on the cloud machine (LESSONS_LEARNED.md 3.12)

host_jitter.basis: the author's estimate for a timer-interrupt loop on a microcontroller with serial and USB interrupts beside it; not measured

host_path.basis: the author's estimate: the microcontroller's own CAN controller, a transmit mailbox away from the bus

bus_transmit.basis: computed: the first drive has its command after 1 frame without stuffing (0.111 ms), the last after 6 frames at the worst stuffing (0.81 ms). The frame times are sourced (c); the order is the author's assumption (d): the commands are sent back to back and win arbitration over the replies (lower identifiers)

drive.basis: the author's estimate from a frame's end to the torque change: up to one period of the drive's outer loop, taken as 1 ms, plus the current's rise (winding L / R: 0.18 mH / 0.4 ohm = 0.45 ms on the X4-36-L and 0.51 mH / 0.41 ohm = 1.24 ms on the X6-60, catalog notes; a closed current loop is faster). With a 500 Hz loop the high end would be 2.50 ms

rate_hold.basis: none: the targets update at the model's 500 Hz

sensor_age_ms.basis: computed from the terms: a drive samples its reply when its command arrives; the reply is used at the first tick after it is back at the controller

if_drive_loop_500_hz.basis: the author's sensitivity: the high end if the drives' outer loop runs at 500 Hz, the slower of the two rates the vendor's driver manuals give (myactuator_mc_driver)

maps_to.rule: k = the total / 2 ms, rounded up to a whole step, at least 1

linux_crash.short: Controlled stop, then stand (once the firmware exists)
linux_crash.detail: The microcontroller keeps the walking loop, the host's velocity request expires and the stop runs from the reference: a controlled stop, then a stand. Meets the requirement once the firmware exists; it is unwritten (COMPUTE.md).

microcontroller_crash.short: Torque-off or frozen drives; a fall when walking
microcontroller_crash.detail: No commands reach the drives until the microcontroller's watchdog restarts it, and Linux has no path to the leg bus. What the drives do without commands is not confirmed (they have a time-out setting): plan on torque-off, which for a walking biped is a fall. Standing, the robot may stay up if the restart is quick and the drives hold.

failure.operator_link_lost: Controlled stop within 1.0 s, then stand: a software rule in whatever runs the walking loop, in every architecture (BEHAVIOR_SPEC.md section 3).

linux_crash.short: Torque-off or the drives' fault reaction; a fall when walking
linux_crash.detail: The EtherCAT master is the thing that crashed: torque-off or the drives' own fault reaction, then a fall when walking. Does not meet the requirement, unless the master runs on a microcontroller, which nobody here has shown.

microcontroller_crash.detail: No microcontroller in the leg loop. If a supervisor is added and it hangs, its fail-safe output decides: an enable line that drops means torque-off.

failure.operator_link_lost: Controlled stop within 1.0 s, then stand: a software rule in whatever runs the walking loop, in every architecture (BEHAVIOR_SPEC.md section 3).

refs.text: Servo target (plan section 2), every physics step (500 Hz)

model.says: A target is an angle, a rate and a feedforward torque folded into one number per drive: ctrl = q + (kv qd + tau) / kp, in front of an ideal PD servo at the holding gains.

refs.text: ctrl = q_ref + dq + (kv qd_ref + tau_ff + dtau) / kp
def command(self, q=None, qd=None, tau=None) -> None:

model.says: The delay: every target, feedforward included, passes through a queue of the last k + 1 targets, so the servos get the target set k physics steps (2 k ms) earlier.

refs.text: queue = deque([p.d.ctrl.copy() for _ in range(steps)], maxlen=steps + 1)

model.says: The ledger's delay readings quoted below were made by the ledger's own copy of the same queue, refilled with the reset's targets at every reset.
k is a whole number of steps, 0 to 10 (0-20 ms): the training environment's random range and the ledger's search range.
Each step: set the target, step the physics, then read the sensors for the next step.
The sensors the controller reads describe the state one physics step (2 ms) earlier.

refs.text: that step's start, one physics step (2 ms) before ``d.qpos``

model.says: The balance feedback is computed every fifth step (100 Hz) and ramped into the targets: one fifth in the step it is computed, all of it four steps (8 ms) later.

The holding gains: kp = the drive's sustained planning torque / 0.01 rad (an assumption), kv = 2 sqrt(kp I), critical damping on the inertia I the drive sees at home with every other drive held: the leg's, not the bare shaft's.

refs.text: kp = np.array([dr.sustained for dr in drives]) / carpet.SERVO_ERROR_RAD
